problemText: An element is located in Period 4 of the periodic table. What does that period number tell you about one of its neutral atoms?
choices: It has 4 valence electrons
It has four occupied electron shells
It belongs to the fourth chemical family, so it behaves like every other Period 4 element
It forms an ion with a 4+ charge
hints: Rows and columns carry different information — one counts shells, the other counts outer electrons.
The period number is the row number, and the row number equals the number of occupied shells.

problemText: Tellurium sits in Period 5, Group 16 of the periodic table. How many valence electrons does a neutral tellurium atom have? Type your answer as a number.
hints: For the main-group columns on the right (Groups 13-18), the valence count is the group number minus 10.
16 − 10 gives the count.

problemText: An unknown element is a colorless, odorless gas that refuses to react with sodium, with fluorine, or with water, even when strongly heated. Which family does it belong to?
choices: Halogens (Group 17) — several halogens are gases at room temperature
Alkali metals (Group 1) — they stay inert until they touch water
Nitrogen family (Group 15) — nitrogen gas is also hard to react
Noble gases (Group 18) — a full outer shell leaves nothing to gain, lose, or share
hints: Reactivity comes from an incomplete outer shell. What does total unreactivity imply about that shell?
One column of the table is defined by already having a full valence shell.

problemText: Consider three elements: beryllium (Period 2, Group 2), boron (Period 2, Group 13), and strontium (Period 5, Group 2). Which two of them are chemical relatives — that is, which two should show the most similar chemical behavior?
choices: Be and B — they sit side by side in Period 2, so they are in the same family
B and Sr — a metalloid and a metal split the difference between the two extremes
Be and Sr — same column, so both have 2 valence electrons and both form 2+ ions
All three, because all three sit in the left half of the table
hints: A chemical family is a column, never a row.
Which two of the three share a group number, and therefore a valence-electron count?

problemText: Germanium sits directly below silicon in Group 14 (Period 4) and lies right on the staircase that divides the table. Which statement best describes germanium?
choices: It is a metalloid with 4 valence electrons, so it conducts electricity partway — better than a nonmetal, worse than a metal
It is a nonmetal with 14 valence electrons, because its group number is 14
It is a transition metal, because it sits in the middle stretch of the table
It is an alkaline earth metal, because it is a solid that conducts some electricity
hints: Two separate reads: the staircase tells you metal, nonmetal, or metalloid; the group number tells you the valence count.
Group 14 → 14 − 10 valence electrons, and sitting ON the staircase means in-between conduction.

problemText: A student applies the "subtract 10" shortcut to iron, which sits in Group 8, gets 8 − 10 = −2 valence electrons, and concludes that the shortcut must be broken. What is the real problem here?
choices: The shortcut works in every column; the student simply subtracted in the wrong order and iron has 2 valence electrons
Iron is a transition metal (Groups 3-12), where electrons fill inner d orbitals, so no group-number shortcut gives its valence count — which is exactly why iron has more than one possible ion charge
Group 8 is a noble-gas column, so iron already has a full shell of 8 valence electrons
The shortcut covers Groups 1-12, so iron has 8 valence electrons and forms only Fe⁸⁺
hints: The subtract-10 rule was stated only for the main-group columns on the right, Groups 13 through 18. Where does Group 8 fall?
Transition metals fill inner d orbitals rather than the outer shell, which is why their charges need Roman numerals instead of a column rule.

problemText: Moving from left to right across a single period of the periodic table, what happens to atomic radius?
choices: It increases, because each step to the right adds another electron
It decreases, because each step adds a proton that pulls the same outer shell in tighter
It stays constant, because every element in the period has the same number of shells
It increases at first and then decreases once the nonmetals begin
hints: Across a period, no new shell opens — the electrons pile into the shell that is already outermost.
With shielding nearly unchanged, extra protons mean a stronger inward pull.

problemText: Oxygen sits in Period 2, Group 16; sulfur sits in Period 3, Group 16. Which atom has the higher electronegativity, and why?
choices: Sulfur — it has more electrons available to attract the shared pair
Sulfur — it is farther down the column, and lower elements are always more reactive
Oxygen — its valence electrons sit in a shell closer to the nucleus with less shielding, so it pulls shared electrons harder
They are equal, because electronegativity is fixed for every member of a group
hints: Electronegativity is the grip an atom keeps on electrons it is sharing. What weakens that grip going down a column?
Down a group: farther out plus more shielding equals a weaker pull.

problemText: Rubidium (Period 5, 37 protons) sits directly below potassium (Period 4, 19 protons) in Group 1. Compared with a potassium atom, a rubidium atom is:
choices: Smaller, because rubidium has 18 more protons pulling its electrons inward
The same size, because both elements have exactly 1 valence electron
Smaller, because rubidium's extra electrons pack together more tightly
Larger, because its valence electron occupies an additional shell, farther out and behind more shielding
hints: Down a group, each step opens a brand-new shell — that is a different story from moving across a period.
New shell plus more shielding beats the extra proton pull, so the radius grows.

problemText: Element Q has successive ionization energies, in kJ/mol, of IE₁ = 496, IE₂ = 4562, IE₃ = 6910, IE₄ = 9543. The enormous jump marks the point where electron removal breaks into the stable noble-gas core. Assuming Q is a main-group element, what is its group number? Type your answer as a number.
hints: Electrons removed BEFORE the giant jump are the loosely held valence electrons; count them first.
IE₂ is about nine times IE₁, so only one electron came off before the wall — and for Groups 1 and 2 the group number equals the valence count.

problemText: Rank lithium (Period 2, Group 1), fluorine (Period 2, Group 17), and cesium (Period 6, Group 1) from LOWEST to HIGHEST first ionization energy.
choices: Cs < Li < F
Li < Cs < F
F < Li < Cs
Cs < F < Li
hints: Ionization energy rises going right across a period and falls going down a group, so it peaks in the top-right corner.
Cesium is the farthest toward the bottom left (cheapest electron to remove); fluorine is nearly top-right (most expensive).

problemText: A student claims: "Sulfur (Period 3, 16 protons) must be bigger than oxygen (Period 2, 8 protons) because sulfur has 8 more electrons — and by the same reasoning sulfur must also be bigger than magnesium (Period 3, 12 protons)." Evaluate both comparisons.
choices: Both conclusions are correct, and electron count is the right explanation for each of them

Sulfur is indeed larger than oxygen, but because it has an extra occupied shell rather than because of raw electron count — and sulfur is actually SMALLER than magnesium, since both share Period 3 and sulfur's 4 extra protons pull that shared shell in tighter
Both conclusions are wrong: sulfur is smaller than oxygen and smaller than magnesium
Sulfur is larger than magnesium but smaller than oxygen, because atomic radius increases from left to right across a period
hints: Handle the two comparisons separately: oxygen and sulfur share a group, while magnesium and sulfur share a period.
Electron count only predicts size when a new SHELL is added. Within one period, proton count decides.

problemText: An atom becomes a cation (a positively charged ion) when it does what?
choices: Gains one or more electrons
Loses one or more electrons
Gains one or more protons
Loses one or more protons
hints: Protons never move in chemistry — they are the element's identity.
Electrons are negative, so removing some leaves the positives in the majority.

problemText: Potassium sits in Group 1 and bromine sits in Group 17. Which pair of monatomic ions do these two elements form?
choices: K⁻ and Br⁺, because the metal collects electrons and the nonmetal releases them
K⁺ and Br⁷⁺, because bromine sheds all 7 of its valence electrons
K⁺ and Br⁻ — potassium loses its single valence electron and bromine gains one to complete its octet
K²⁺ and Br²⁻, because monatomic ions always carry a charge of 2
hints: Metals on the left have low ionization energy and lose electrons; nonmetals on the right have high electronegativity and gain them.
Group 1 → 1 valence electron to give away; Group 17 → 7 valence electrons, one short of eight.

problemText: Oxygen is in Group 16 and forms a monatomic ion. What is the correct symbol AND name for that ion?
choices: O²⁻, the oxide ion
O²⁺, the oxygen ion
O⁶⁻, the oxide ion
O²⁻, the oxygen ion
hints: Group 16 means 6 valence electrons, and a nonmetal gains (8 − 6) of them.
Monatomic anions swap their ending to -ide; only cations keep the plain element name.

problemText: A monatomic ion of an unknown main-group element carries a 3− charge and contains 18 electrons. How many protons does that ion have? Type your answer as a number.
hints: A 3− charge means the ion holds 3 more electrons than it has protons.
Protons = 18 − 3.

problemText: O²⁻ (8 protons), Na⁺ (11 protons), and Al³⁺ (13 protons) each contain exactly 10 electrons. Which of the three is the LARGEST, and why?
choices: Al³⁺ — the biggest charge means it takes up the most space
O²⁻ — only 8 protons are holding those 10 electrons, so the grip is weakest and the electron cloud spreads widest
Na⁺ — sodium is a metal, and metal particles are always the largest
All three are identical in size, because all three contain 10 electrons
hints: Same electron count does not mean same size — compare how many protons are pulling on that shared crowd of 10.
Fewest protons = weakest pull = biggest ion.

problemText: Both iron(II) chloride and iron(III) chloride are real compounds. A student objects: "Iron would have to be in Group 2 and Group 3 at the same time for that to work, which is impossible, so one of those compounds must be fake." What is the correct analysis?
choices: Iron is a transition metal, and transition metals have more than one stable charge — Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺ are both real, the Roman numeral names which one is present, and the group-to-charge shortcut simply does not apply to Groups 3-12
Only iron(III) chloride is real; the II in the other name is a typo for the number of chloride ions
Iron sits in Group 8, so its only possible ion is Fe⁸⁺ and both names are wrong
The Roman numeral counts the iron atoms in the formula, not the charge, so neither name says anything about iron's ion
hints: The group → charge map was stated for main-group elements only. Which block does iron belong to?
Roman numerals appear in a name precisely because the element's charge cannot be read off its column.
